The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

Sergeant Marrow's eyes go to the slip before they go to him. She doesn't pick it up. She tilts her head and reads the seal where it lies, the way people read a thing they've seen forged before, and something in her shoulders lets go a little.

"Zaranda's." It isn't a question. The chalk scratches *WORGEN* onto the board under a column of other names, then *TETH.* and a stroke for *on foot*. Under her elbow lies a thick ledger, open, where the chalkboard names get copied in ink at the end of a shift. As she shifts her arm, James sees the margin of the left-hand page: most of the lines are bare, but beside four or five names someone has drawn a small, careful cross in chalk. It isn't ink and it isn't a tally mark. Just the crosses.

"Work, bed, meal." She pushes the slip back across the trestle with two fingers. "The Fist hires at the Seatower, mornings, if you don't mind wearing red and being spat at. Beds on this bridge are cheap and they've got fleas. Inside the walls they cost more and they've still got fleas." Her gaze flicks past his shoulder, to the barrel and the lean man's busy hands, and comes back flat. "And whatever you heard about luck in the Gate, keep your hand on your purse past that barrel."

Behind him the cards slap down. "There she is! Oh, *so* close, friend, so close. Again?"

At his boots the cat has sat down, tail curled over its paws, and its answer arrives as plain, wordless pressure behind his eyes: *One. Not moving. Wet wool, onions. Watching the barrel-man. Not you.*

The sergeant holds out her ink-stained palm, flat on the trestle.

"Two copper, on foot. Next."

Sergeant Marrow sweeps the two coppers off the trestle into a tin box without counting them. The chalk is already moving to the next line when the question reaches her, and it stops.

She looks at him properly for the first time, the way a sergeant looks at a man who has asked a sensible question at the end of a long day.

"Haskett's. Halfway along, past the chandler, narrow house with green shutters." She taps the chalk against the board twice. "Widow runs it. Bolts the door at midnight and keeps the boots in the kitchen where she can see them. Six copper a night, and if you're not in by the bolt you sleep on the step." She pauses, as if deciding whether to say the next part. "Tell her Marrow sent you. She'll give you the back room. It doesn't look onto the river."

She doesn't say why that matters. Her eyes go down to the ledger, then back up, and for a moment it looks like she's about to ask him something. Instead she lifts her chin at the man behind him.

"Next."

The queue pushes James forward onto the span itself. The road narrows between the leaning houses, and the barrel is right there on his left, close enough to touch. A drover with a sunburnt neck has just found the lady. His mates slap his back, and the lean man in the waistcoat laughs as though losing is the best part of his evening. "Eye like a hawk, friend! Fair's fair." He dips into a fat little purse at his belt and counts the winnings into the drover's palm.

He pays in copper, a dozen worn pennies for a game that was staked in silver. James has watched a great many tables pay out, and nobody pays a winner in copper when silver is on the barrel unless the copper is what he's meant to hand over.

The drover doesn't care. He shoves the coins into his pocket, grinning.

At James's boots, the cat's fur rises along its spine in one slow ripple. Its answer arrives sharper than before: *Coins. Those coins. Wet cellar, old candles. Wrong.* A beat, then calmer: *Wool-and-onions still there. Still watching barrel-man. Not moving.*

Behind them the chalk scratches on. Ahead, the bridge runs on under its lamps toward the walls of the Lower City, and somewhere along it are green shutters and a widow who bolts her door at midnight.

James leaves the barrel behind. The cards slap down at his back, the lean man's voice rises and falls, and James keeps walking.

The chestnut seller is a stooped woman with a brazier and a tin scoop. "Two copper the twist." She folds hot chestnuts into a cone of old broadsheet. Their skins are split and black at the edges. While she does it, the barrel and the drovers sit at the edge of James's eye: the sunburnt man taking backslaps, one of his mates pointing at the cards and making an argument with his hands.

It takes a few minutes. Then the drover claps the arguing mate on the shoulder, says something that makes them all laugh, and turns up the bridge alone. He's walking with the loose, rolling ease of a man who has had a good evening and a pint before it.

The drover looks at the offered chestnuts, then at James, with the friendly suspicion of a countryman on a city bridge. Then he takes three, juggling them because they're hot.

"Ta. Wasn't eye, mind. Luck." He grins and blows on his fingers. Then the silver between James's fingers catches the lamplight, and he squints at it. "Ten for one? That's square, that's not ahead." He's already digging in his pocket, though. "Square suits me. Copper's a weight in the pocket and the alehouses over the water'll want silver anyway." He counts them out into James's palm with a thumb, one at a time and moving his lips. Ten worn pennies. He holds his hand out for the silver, and when he has it he bites it, out of habit rather than doubt. "Corlin. Wool carts, out of Beregost, if you're ever wanting wool." He tips his head at the cone. "Ta for the nuts."

He sets off. Three steps later his bootlace snaps. Corlin swears cheerfully, stoops to knot it on the cobbles, and a porter with a crate nearly walks into him. Then he's up and gone into the crowd toward the far end of the span, with two of the pennies still in his pocket.

The coppers sit in James's palm. They're warm, the way coins are warm from a man's pocket, and they're dull brown and worn nearly smooth. Under his thumb each one has a small roughness at the rim, a notch where a coin's edge ought to be plain.

The cat's answer comes in two parts. *Barrel-man didn't look. Hands busy, new man at the barrel, talking.* A pause, and then the pressure sharpens. *Wool-and-onions looked. Watched the sunburnt one go past him. Watched you give the shiny coin. Then back to the barrel.* Another beat. *Still not moving.*

The chestnut woman's brazier pops behind him. Up the bridge, past the chandler, somewhere, are green shutters.

The chestnuts are good: sweet and floury, too hot to eat quickly. James eats them as he walks. The bridge narrows and widens again as the houses lean in and draw back, and the crowd thins as the evening goes on. Porters pass with empty frames on their backs, a girl hauls a water-yoke, and two Fist men walk the other way without looking at anyone. The chandler's is easy to find. Its window is lined with tallow dips and beeswax tapers, and a good brass lamp hangs over the door so passers-by can see the stock. James puts his back to the shop's planking, under the light.

He turns the penny over.

The faces show him very little. One side has the ghost of a ship, its sails worn down to a smear. The other is rubbed nearly blank by a thousand thumbs. It's an ordinary Gate penny, older than most, with nothing scratched or stamped into either face.

The notch at the rim is different, and in good light it isn't really a notch. James tilts the coin until the lamplight runs along its edge. Something has been pressed into the rim, not cut. The copper around it is pushed up in a tiny bead on either side, the way soft metal swells when it's struck. The mark is about the size of a grain of barley and shaped like a branch with tines: two sharp points curving up from a stem, and a third, shorter one. It's darker than the copper around it, close to black, as if it were burned in rather than punched. Whoever made it did it carefully. It sits in the same place on the rim as the roughness he felt with his thumb on the others.

It is an antler.

A black antler is Beshaba's sign. She is the Maid of Misfortune, the Lady's sister and her opposite. Anyone who has knelt in a house of Tymora has seen that antler painted small and upside down on the warding-boards by the doors, where it's put to keep her out.

He brings the coin up to his nose. A man's nose gets copper, old sweat and the river, and nothing he can swear to beyond that. The cat smelled a wet cellar and old candles. To him the coin smells like a coin. It's still warm, though. He's had it in his fist for the whole walk, so that proves nothing yet. But the night air off the Chionthar is cool on his knuckles, and the penny hasn't cooled at all.

As he lowers his hand, the cone of chestnuts tips in the crook of his arm. One rolls out over the broadsheet's edge, bounces once on the cobbles and drops into the gutter-channel that runs along the shopfronts toward the river.

The cat came with him the whole way, a pace behind his heel. Now it sits at his boot with its head turned back down the bridge. Its answer comes thinner than before, stretched over the distance:

*Far now. Can't smell him. Can see: dark between the shut stalls. Same shape, same place.* A pause. *Barrel-man loud. New person losing.* Then, closer and plainer: *That coin. Same as the others. I still don't like it in your hand.*

A little farther along, past the chandler's, the lamplight falls on a narrow house wedged between a cooper's and a shuttered pie shop. Its shutters are painted green.

The door opens on the second knock, wide enough for a face and a candle. Behind it is a hall too narrow for two people to pass, and it smells of boiled onions and lye soap. The woman holding the candle is about sixty, small and broad, with a man's grey cardigan buttoned over her apron and her sleeves pushed up past the elbow. She looks James over from hat to boots, then looks down at the cat, then back at him.

"Ilse sent you?" She takes the six copper and counts them in her palm with one finger, the way Corlin did, though she does it faster. "Then you're Ilse's, and that's the back room. She always sends her lot to the back. Says the front's too loud for anyone who's been on the road all day. Carts all night, and the drunks singing their way home over the water." The coins go into her apron pocket. "Haskett. Widow, yes. Come in, mind the step, it's lower than it looks."

The step is lower than it looks. James knows to watch for it, so it doesn't catch him.

She leads him down the hall past a front parlour with two boarders in it. One is an old man asleep in a chair, the other a young woman darning a stocking by the fire, and she doesn't look up. They come to a kitchen at the back. It's warm, with a black range and a pot muttering on the hob, and against the wall a row of boots stands in pairs on a strip of sacking: four pairs, each with a twist of paper tucked into the cuff and a name written on it.

"Boots there when you go up. Name in the cuff, I'll give you paper. Nobody's walked out of this house in someone else's yet." She nods at a narrow stair going up beside the range. "Room's at the top, on the left. Bed, basin, a hook for your coat. The window's on the cooper's yard. You'll hear him start at dawn and there's no helping that." She looks at the cat again. It has sat down by the range as if it was invited. "That one can stay if it keeps off the table. We've got mice that need a talking-to."

She lifts the lid off the pot and stirs. Steam rolls up, pease and ham bone.

"There's supper if you want it. Bowl and bread, two copper. It's hot now. In an hour it won't be."

The two coppers go onto the scrubbed table and straight into her apron pocket. Widow Haskett nods him to the bench under the window. She ladles the bowl full to the brim, the way a woman does when she'd sooner give too much than hear about it, and cuts bread off a round loaf held against her chest. She hands him a twist of paper and a stub of pencil from the dresser. WORGEN goes into the cuff, and the boots go at the end of the row on the sacking, a fifth pair.

The pease is thick, salty and good, with shreds of ham off the bone. She sees him eat the first few spoonfuls without a word and takes it as the compliment it is. She sits down across from him with a basket of mending.

At the question she doesn't look up. She bites off a thread.

"Bad company? It's noisy, that's what it is. Carts on the front till all hours, and the lads off the boats singing their way home." She holds a sock up to the lamp, finds the hole and frowns at it. "Ilse's careful with the ones she sends me. Always has been, since she got the south gate. Two years, near enough. She says road folk sleep badly as it is without wheels under their window." She threads the needle on the first try. "Sergeants are people too, love or not. Some of them notice things."

She says it plainly. She believes every word of it, and she has nothing more to add. The needle goes in and out.

"You'll want the end of that loaf, I suppose. Men off the road always do." She nudges it across without waiting for an answer. "Water jug's on the stair if you want it upstairs. Don't take the lamp, take a candle. I've had one lamp go off that stair already this year."

Out in the front parlour a log settles in the grate. The old man in the chair snores once and stops.

By the range, the cat has folded itself into a loaf of its own, eyes half shut and ears turned toward the hall. Its answer comes slow and even: *Door shut. Street: feet going past, a cart, a woman laughing. Nobody stopping.* A pause. *Mice in the wall behind the dresser. Three. Later.*

The bowl is still half full, and there's more bread than any one man needs. It's not yet eight, and the bolt doesn't go across until midnight.

Widow Haskett watches the bowl come back wiped clean and gives a short nod, the kind a cook gives when the job is done. She doesn't say anything about the compliment. She pulls the bowl to her side of the table and stacks it on the dresser without getting up.

At the question her hands keep moving. The needle goes in and out of the heel of the sock at the same pace as before, and the thread draws through and tightens with nothing like a pause. She's a woman who has darned ten thousand socks while answering questions about the weather.

"Waistcoat. With the cards." She snips the thread with her teeth. "Since the thaw, near enough. Before him it was a fellow with dice and a bad eye, and the Fist moved him on in the autumn. There's always one. Sometimes two." She turns the sock right side out and looks at it under the lamp. "Him at the south end, and there's a woman with shells and a pea further over toward the Rock, some evenings. More of them since the boats came down from upriver. Everybody wants a quick silver."

She drops the sock in the basket and picks up a shirt with a torn cuff.

"The lads from the camps stand round that barrel half the day. They ought to be at the docks asking for work." She doesn't say it unkindly, only the way she'd say the step was low. "My Haskett lost a good cart-horse to dice once, years back. A man at a fair in Rivington, very friendly voice." The needle finds the cuff. "That's what I know about card men. Friendly till they've got your horse."

Her hands stay steady and her face stays plain. As far as James can tell she has nothing more to give him.

By the range the cat opens one eye. *Street: a cart. Two feet, a dog. Nobody stopping.* The eye closes again.

The kitchen is warm and the pot ticks on the hob. Beside the stair, the candle stubs stand in a row on the dresser, waiting.

"Night." Widow Haskett doesn't look up from the cuff. "Bolt's at midnight. Candle, not the lamp."

The candle stub catches at the range and James shields it with his hand. The cat goes up the stair ahead of him, quick and silent, and waits on the top step with its tail curled round its feet. The cup clinks against the water jug, and then the door at the top on the left shuts behind them both.

The room is the size of a generous cupboard: bed, washstand with a chipped basin, a hook on the back of the door, one window. Below it the cooper's yard is a square of dark. Barrel staves are stacked against the wall, a cart stands with its shafts down, and nobody is in it. The curtain is a length of brown wool on a string. James draws it across and sets the candle on the basin stand.

The knot in the silk is tight and takes a moment. Ten pennies slide out into his palm, still warm. He sets one on the bare wood at the far edge of the stand, a forearm's length from the rest.

The cat jumps up onto the bed, stretches its neck over the edge of the stand and breathes in, nose working. It does the heap first, then the lone penny, then the heap again.

*Same. All same. Not stronger, not weaker.* A pause while it sniffs again, as if to make sure. *Like one smell cut into ten pieces.*

James draws the Lady's coin out on its cord. It's warm the way it always is, from lying against his chest, and he knows its weight as well as his own hand. He holds it a hand's breadth above the lone penny and waits.

For a moment nothing happens. Then, in still air with his hand steady, the coin begins to turn on its cord. It turns slowly, the way a hanging thing turns in a draught, except no draught moves the candle flame. It comes round until it hangs edge-on to the penny below and stops there, its face turned away. He lowers it a finger's breadth, then another. The cord twists a little more under his fingers to keep the coin edge-on, and holds it there.

The warmth goes out of it. It doesn't turn cold, but it cools to the temperature of the room, like any coin left on a table. That's the one thing it has never done in all the time he's worn it.

The penny on the wood stays as it was: dull, worn and warm, sitting there like an ordinary coin.

On the bed the cat's ears have gone flat. *Smell didn't change. Theirs stays cellar.* Its tail lashes once. *Yours stopped smelling of you. Now it smells like... stone in the sun. Dry. Hot.* A beat. *Don't like it either. Different not-like.*

He lifts the coin a hand's breadth higher. It turns back on its cord, slowly, until it hangs face-on again, and the warmth comes back into it over a few breaths.

Then the cat's head comes up and swings toward the curtain and the front of the house beyond it.

*Front door. Someone stopped.* The pressure behind his eyes sharpens. *Wet wool. Onions.* A pause, and then a knock below: three raps, unhurried, the kind a man gives when he expects to be let in. *Him. The one from between the stalls.*

Down in the kitchen a chair scrapes. Widow Haskett's slippers shuffle along the narrow hall toward the door.

James hears all of it. The house is narrow and the hall carries sound like a pipe.

"Evening, Mistress." It's a man's voice, low and unhurried, with a Gate accent rubbed thin at the edges. "Sorry to call so late."

"It's not late. It's gone eight. Late's midnight." Widow Haskett doesn't open the door any wider. "What do you want?"

"Word with one of your lodgers. Came in maybe an hour since. Tallish, hat, an old soldier's cloak off the southern road. Cat at his heel." He pauses. "Grey cat."

"I've got lodgers. What they look like is their own business."

"Fair." He doesn't push. He sounds like a man who has stood on a lot of doorsteps and been told no on most of them. "Only he bought a drover's winnings off him tonight. Penhallow's coppers, off the barrel at the south end. Silver for copper, right there on the bridge." Another pause. "There's people I do errands for who'd like to know who's collecting Penhallow's take now. If it's him, they'd sooner hear it from him civil than find out some other way."

"I don't carry messages for people you do errands for, Hobb."

So she knows him. She says the name the way she'd name a neighbour's dog that keeps getting into the bins.

"No, Mistress. Course not." There's a smile in it, a tired one. "Just tell him I asked. Nothing nasty. I'll be on the pie shop step till the bell goes for ten. After that he can ask for me at the Tar Barrel over the water, if he likes."

The cat's report runs under the voices, steady and close: *Thin man. Wet wool, onions, and beer from before. Hands open, nothing in them. Hobb lowers the pie onto its paper on his knee and looks at James side-on for a while, measuring him.

He pauses before the next part and turns the crust in his fingers.

He says it mildly, as though he's still a bit annoyed. "And you're not the only one who's been at his barrel with questions. A girl from the camps came at him last week, about a brother. Shouting. Penhallow laughed at her and gave her a copper for her trouble." He shrugs. "She threw it in the river. I remember that because hardly anyone does."

James steps up when the chalk taps, and keeps his eyes on the sergeant and off the barrel, though the slap of the cards is hard to ignore.

"James Worgen," he says, and sets his regimental pay slip on the table so she can see the Tethyrian seal without having to ask. "Out of Tethyr by way of the southern road. My business is finding work, a bed, and a meal I didn't cook myself. In that order, if the Gate allows."

Without looking down, he thinks to the cat: *Stay by my boots. Keep your ears on whatever's back there, and tell me if it moves.*

James sets two copper on the trestle and tucks the pay slip back inside his coat.

"Fleas I can live with. Thieves I'd rather meet on my own terms." He nods, a soldier's nod to a sergeant at the end of a long shift. "If a man wanted a bed on this bridge where the landlord doesn't sell his guests' boots in the morning, where would you send him?"

He doesn't look at the ledger again, but he remembers the crosses.

To the cat, silently: *Good. Keep him in the corner of your eye. If he follows the barrel-man, or follows me, tell me.*

James keeps walking past the barrel without breaking stride. He doesn't look at the cards, though it costs him something. Ten paces on he stops at a stall still lit for the evening trade and buys a twist of roasted chestnuts, which puts the barrel and the drover at the edge of his eye.

When the sunburnt drover finally peels away from his mates, pockets heavy and grinning, James falls into step beside him and offers the chestnuts.

"Well played back there. Good eye." He holds up a silver piece between two fingers. "Do me a favour, friend? I'm short of copper for a widow's bed, and she won't break silver. I'll give you this for ten of those pennies he paid you. You come out ahead twice in one night."

To the cat, silently: *Stay on the barrel-man and the wool-and-onions one. If either of them watches us make this trade, I want to know.*

James pockets nine of the pennies and keeps one in his fist. He walks on up the bridge at an easy pace, eating a chestnut, until he reaches a lamp bright enough to read by, close to the chandler's.

There he stops with his back to a shopfront, turns the penny over under the light, and looks at it properly. He wants to know what the notch at the rim is, whether there's anything stamped or scratched on either face, and whether it smells of cellar and old candles to a man's nose as well as a cat's. He gives it a good look, the way he'd check a card he suspected of being marked.

To the cat, silently: *Come with me, but keep an ear back toward wool-and-onions. If he leaves the barrel, I want to know which way he goes.*

James closes his fist on the penny and stands a moment longer under the chandler's lamp. A black antler, on the coins a cardsharp pays out to winners. *Of course,* he thinks. *Of course that's the first thing the Gate shows me.*

He takes a scrap of silk from the component pouch, wraps all ten pennies in it, knots it, and puts the bundle in a coat pocket on its own, away from his purse and well away from the Lady's coin on its cord. He touches the coin at his throat through his shirt once. It's an old habit, and it feels more like a question now.

To the cat, silently: *I don't like them either. They stay wrapped. Come on. Green shutters.*

He walks the last stretch to the narrow house between the cooper's and the pie shop and knocks at the door. When it opens he takes his hat off.

"Evening. Widow Haskett? Sergeant Marrow at the checkpoint sent me. She said you might have the back room, the one that doesn't look onto the river." He holds out six copper from his own purse, not from the bundle. "James Worgen. I'll be in well before the bolt, and my boots can sleep in your kitchen."

"Supper, gladly." James counts two more copper onto the table, again from his own purse, and sits where she points. He unlaces his boots while the bowl is filled, writes WORGEN on the paper she gives him, and sets the boots on the sacking at the end of the row.

He eats the first few spoonfuls in silence. He means it as a compliment, and it is one. Then, between mouthfuls, in the easy voice of a man making conversation with his landlady:

"Sergeant Marrow seemed to care which way my window faced. Most sergeants I've known don't trouble themselves that far over a stranger's bed." He tears the bread. "Has the river been bad company lately, Mistress Haskett?"

To the cat, silently: *Mice can wait. Keep an ear on the front door and the street. If anyone stops outside these shutters tonight, wake me.*

James finishes the bowl properly, mops it clean with the end of the loaf, and pushes it back across the table with a nod of thanks.

"That's the best thing I've eaten since Beregost." He leans back against the window frame. "There's a fellow at the south end with a barrel and three cards. Fancy waistcoat, friendly voice, pays his winners in copper. Is he a fixture on the bridge, or new this season?"

He asks it lightly, the way a man asks about the weather, and watches her hands rather than her face.

To the cat, silently: *Keep listening. Once I've got her answer, we go up, and I want your nose on those pennies again where nobody can see us.*

"Friendly till they've got your horse." James almost smiles. "I'll remember that. Good night, Mistress Haskett, and thank you for the supper."

He takes a candle stub from the dresser, lights it at the range, fills a cup from the water jug on the stair, and climbs to the room at the top on the left. Once the door is shut behind him and the cat, he checks the window onto the cooper's yard and draws the curtain across it. Then he sits on the edge of the bed with the candle on the basin stand and unknots the silk.

He sets one penny apart on the wooden edge of the stand, well away from the others.

To the cat, silently: *Your nose, please. Is it the same smell on all of them, or stronger on some? And tell me if anything about it changes while I do this.*

Then, slowly, he draws the Lady's coin out on its cord. He doesn't touch it to the penny. He holds it a hand's breadth above, then lower, and watches the coin and the copper both, and feels for any change in the warmth against his fingers.

James sweeps the nine pennies and the lone one back into the silk and knots it fast. The bundle goes into his coat pocket and the Lady's coin back under his shirt, warm again against his chest. He pinches out the candle, so no light shows under the door.

He eases the door open a crack and stands just inside it in his stockinged feet, one hand resting on the rod at his belt. He doesn't draw it. He's listening down the stairwell.

To the cat, silently: *Go down. Quiet, low, stay by the range where she'd expect you. I want to hear what he says to her and what she says back. If he asks for me by name, or describes me, tell me at once. Don't let him see you watching.*

James comes down the stair in his stockings, quietly for the old man's sake, and stops two steps above her so they're nearly eye to eye.

"I do. On the bridge, as you say, and none of it comes through your door." He keeps his voice as low as hers. "I bought ten pennies off a drover, Mistress. That's all I did. I'd rather tell this Hobb so myself tonight than have him and his errand-givers wondering about it over breakfast." He tips his head toward the bolt. "I'll be back well before midnight. If I'm not, my boots can keep my place in your kitchen, and you can let the room."

He takes the paper twist out of the cuff, pulls his boots on and laces them by the range. Then he settles his cloak and checks that the silk bundle is in its own pocket and the rod is at his belt.

To the cat, silently: *Come with me, but not at my heel. Get up high, along the shopfronts or a sill, somewhere you can see the pie shop step and the street both ways. Watch his hands, and watch for anyone else who's watching us. If a second person turns up, tell me before I see them.*

At the door he waits for her to draw the bolt. "Thank you for not carrying his message," he says. "Sounds like you've had practice."

James sits down on the step beside him, leaving a good arm's length between them, and rests his forearms on his knees so both hands stay in the lamplight, empty.

"Neither, as it happens. I've never met Penhallow, and I don't much like copper." He says it easily, a man with nothing to sell. "I've sat at a lot of tables, Hobb. When a man stakes silver and pays his winner in worn pennies, it isn't generosity. It's a delivery. The drover was carrying something and didn't know it, so I bought it off him to see what it was. Curiosity, and a cheap one at a silver."

He lets that sit a moment and watches Hobb's face rather than the street. The cat has the street.

"So here's my question for your people, and you can carry it back as civil as you like. Do they want to know who's *collecting* Penhallow's coppers, or who's *receiving* them? I'd guess the drover isn't the first who walked off that bridge with a pocketful." He tips his head slightly. "And do your people know what's pressed into the rims, or are they only counting where the copper goes?"

He doesn't bring out the bundle.

To the cat, silently: *Watch his hands when I say "rims." And keep the street. Anyone who lingers too long, tell me.*

"Worgen. James Worgen. You had it at the door, so I'll not make you pretend you didn't." He says it without heat.

He takes his time over the rest, looking out at the lamps on the span rather than at Hobb.

"A mark, pressed into the edge where a thumb finds it and an eye doesn't. Small as a barley grain. Burned dark, done careful, the same spot on every coin." He holds up a hand with two fingers crooked and a third shorter. "An antler. Black. Anyone who's knelt in a house of Tymora has seen it painted upside down by the doors to keep someone out. The Lady's sister. The one who isn't luck."

He lets that land, then turns back to Hobb.

"So your people can count, and they should. But I'd tell them that Penhallow's friend may not be the sort who pays a share to anybody. He may be the sort who's handing out misfortune by the dozen to drovers and camp lads, one penny at a time, and calling it a game." He keeps his voice level. "I'm not collecting it. I've half a mind to find out where it goes."

He rests his forearms on his knees again.

"Two things for the road, Hobb, and I'll owe you a pie for them. Which morning does he walk to Rivington? And the girl from the camps, the one who threw his copper in the river. Do you know her name, or which camp?"

*To the cat, silently:* Watch his face when I say "the Lady's sister." Keep the street. If anyone's been standing still too long out there, tell me now.

## Player's note: James Worgen, session 1

**What worked**

- **Tone and texture.** This felt like Baldur's Gate. The bridge, the chestnut cone made of old broadsheet, the low step, and the boots in the kitchen with names in the cuffs. The world felt lived-in without lingering on it.
- **The NPCs were the best part.** Marrow, Haskett and Hobb each had their own voice, their own business and their own limits. Haskett refusing to carry Hobb's message, then bolting the door hours early, said more than any exposition could. Hobb being tired, mild and annoyed at losing Penhallow in the lanes made him a person, not a quest-giver.
- **The clue trail was layered and fair.** First the copper paid out on a silver stake, which I could catch because I play cards. Then the cat's smell. Then the antler on the rim. Then the Lady's coin turning edge-on and going cold. Each step rewarded attention, and nothing was handed over. The Beshaba link fits my patron perfectly and makes this feel like *my* story. The chalk crosses in Marrow's ledger and the camp girl's missing brother are good seeds I want to pull on. I also suspect they connect to the drowned-men thread, and I like that I can only suspect it.
- **The cat.** Its sensory, clipped telepathic voice ("Like one smell cut into ten pieces") was excellent, and it reliably answered exactly what I asked it to watch.
- **The temptation was handled with restraint.** It was in the background of every scene and never forced.

**What broke or felt off**

- **Money didn't match the sheet from line one.** My hero file says 350 gold; the records showed 315 gp, 315 sp and 350 cp. After that, the deductions were tracked carefully, but the starting figure needs fixing or explaining.
- **Sheet versus records inconsistencies:**
  - Healing Light is "up to 5 dice at a time" on my sheet but "up to 4" in the records.
  - The rapier is +5 on the sheet and +2 in the records. The +2 is RAW-correct for a warlock, so the sheet is the problem, but someone should reconcile it.
  - Hex and Guiding Bolt are listed as 1st level, while all my slots are 3rd.
- **Log noise.** The bowl of pease, the cup of water and the candle stub were added as inventory items. The Seatower got "New place" because Marrow mentioned it, and Rivington because Hobb did. This clutters the records and dilutes the real signals, like "Lead: the antler-marked coppers."
- **The Perception roll at the stair was unnecessary.** The house had just been described as carrying sound like a pipe, and my passive 11 beats DC 10. Rolling only when it matters is the stated rule, so this should have been a free success.
- **The out-of-game note in the coin scene** explained why there was no roll. It wasn't needed, and it broke the moment a little.

**What was missing**

- Very little for a first session. It was all investigation and conversation, and that suited the character, but I never got a feel for danger. One visible threat on the horizon would raise the stakes.
- The session ended on my questions to Hobb, so I'd like next time to open with his answers rather than a time skip.

Overall, this was a strong opening. The GM listened to what I was curious about and built the mystery from it instead of steering me toward a hook.

Yes, a few. Most were my own choice, which I think is a good sign, but they're worth naming.

**The barrel.** This was the big one. When Penhallow's cards slapped down and he called "Find the lady," I wanted to step up and play. I didn't want to win. I wanted to watch his hands at close range, see the lift, maybe catch the switch and call it out loud in front of the drovers. A card-proficient ex-gambler is exactly the man who could do that. I didn't, because the ban is the character, and even standing at the barrel to "just watch" felt like the first step James swore off. So I walked past and bought chestnuts. That restraint felt right, but part of me hopes the game makes me pay for it later, or tests it harder. A situation where reading a cheat's hands is the only way to save someone would be a real dilemma.

**Marrow's ledger.** I saw the chalk crosses and badly wanted to ask about them. I held back because it was a stranger asking a tired Fist sergeant about her private marks in a public queue. I thought she'd close up, or worse, remember me as nosy. She almost asked *me* something, and I let that pass too. I regret it slightly. I want to go back to her alone, off shift.

**Tailing the watcher.** When the cat first flagged wool-and-onions between the stalls, I thought about doubling back, putting on a different face with Mask of Many Faces, and watching *him*. I chose the penny trade instead because it felt less obvious. It worked out, since he came to me, but I gave up the initiative.

**The coin touching the penny.** In my room I deliberately didn't let the Lady's coin touch the antler penny. I wanted to, out of curiosity. But it had just gone cold and turned its face away, and that read as a clear "no" from my patron. I didn't want to find out what happens if I ignore her on day one.

**Magic in general.** I cast nothing all session. That was mostly appropriate, since the canon says a strange caster on the street frightens people. But there were moments for Friends on Hobb, or Prestidigitation to clean my hands of the penny smell, where I hesitated because I wasn't sure how visible or costly the world would treat them. A small early sign of how ordinary cantrips land in the Gate would help me judge.

None of these were blocked by the game. The interface never stopped me. They were all character or caution, and the scenes made the hesitation feel meaningful rather than arbitrary.

Porters pass with empty frames on their backs, a girl hauls a water-yoke, and two Fist men walk the other way without looking at anyone. The chandler's is easy to find. Its window is lined with tallow dips and beeswax tapers, and a good brass lamp hangs over the door so passers-by can see the stock. James puts his back to the shop's planking, under the light.

He turns the penny over.

The faces show him very little. One side has the ghost of a ship, its sails worn down to a smear. The other is rubbed nearly blank by a thousand thumbs. It's an ordinary Gate penny, older than most, with nothing scratched or stamped into either face.

The notch at the rim is different, and in good light it isn't really a notch. James tilts the coin until the lamplight runs along its edge. Something has been pressed into the rim, not cut. The copper around it is pushed up in a tiny bead on either side, the way soft metal swells when it's struck. The mark is about the size of a grain of barley and shaped like a branch with tines: two sharp points curving up from a stem, and a third, shorter one. It's darker than the copper around it, close to black, as if it were burned in rather than punched. Whoever made it did it carefully. It sits in the same place on the rim as the roughness he felt with his thumb on the others.

It is an antler.

A black antler is Beshaba's sign. She is the Maid of Misfortune, the Lady's sister and her opposite. Anyone who has knelt in a house of Tymora has seen that antler painted small and upside down on the warding-boards by the doors, where it's put to keep her out.

He brings the coin up to his nose. A man's nose gets copper, old sweat and the river, and nothing he can swear to beyond that. The cat smelled a wet cellar and old candles. To him the coin smells like a coin. It's still warm, though. He's had it in his fist for the whole walk, so that proves nothing yet. But the night air off the Chionthar is cool on his knuckles, and the penny hasn't cooled at all.

As he lowers his hand, the cone of chestnuts tips in the crook of his arm. One rolls out over the broadsheet's edge, bounces once on the cobbles and drops into the gutter-channel that runs along the shopfronts toward the river.

"Ten pennies." She lets out a breath through her nose. "Well, that's a daft thing to be sent for at this hour. But it's your evening." She takes the twist of paper from him when he pulls it out of the cuff. She doesn't put it away, just turns it in her fingers while he sits on the bench by the range and laces his boots. "Room's paid. I'll not let it out from under a man who's paid. You're in by the bolt or you're on the step, and that's the whole of it."

The cat comes off the warm bricks and is at the kitchen door before James has finished his second lace.

She goes down the hall ahead of him. At his thanks she stops with her hand on the bolt and gives him a short, dry look over her shoulder.

"Thirty-one years of lodgers. Every one of them's got a cousin who wants a word." The bolt draws back with a clack. "Mind you don't bring him back with you."

The door opens onto the bridge. The evening is cool and smells of river after the kitchen. The lamps are lit end to end now, and the traffic has thinned to the odd cart and late walkers. The cat goes past James's boots and is gone before the door shuts behind him. A grey streak runs along the bottom of the cooper's wall, then up a drainpipe in three quick pulls, and settles onto the bracket of the pie shop's hanging sign, a painted crust above the door, dark against the dark.

Its report comes almost at once, close and clear: *Up. On the sign. See the step, see the street both ways.* A pause. *Him, on the step. Eating. One hand pie, one hand nothing. Knife still at his back, under the coat.* Another pause, longer, while it looks. *Street: cart going toward the big rock. Two in red, far, walking away. A dog at the fish-scraps. Nobody stopped. Nobody looking at you but him.*

Two yards to James's left, the pie shop is shuttered for the evening. On its worn step sits a thin man in a damp wool coat with his knees up, eating a pie out of a fold of paper, and a pie-shop smell comes off him with the wet wool. He's maybe forty, with a narrow face and a nose broken once and left that way. He looks up when the door opens. He doesn't stand, but he moves along the step to make room, the way a man does on a bench.

"Evening." That's Hobb's voice from the hall, low and unhurried. He looks James over once, hat, cloak, boots, and the empty air at his heel where the cat ought to be. Whatever he makes of that, he keeps it to himself. "Kind of you to come out. Saves us both a walk to the Tar Barrel." He brushes crumbs off his knee and waits a moment before he gets to it. "So. The people I run for want to know whether you're Penhallow's new collector, or just a man who likes copper."

James sits down on the step beside him, leaving a good arm's length between them, and rests his forearms on his knees so both hands stay in the lamplight, empty.

"Neither, as it happens. I've never met Penhallow, and I don't much like copper." He says it easily, a man with nothing to sell. "I've sat at a lot of tables, Hobb. When a man stakes silver and pays his winner in worn pennies, it isn't generosity. It's a delivery. The drover was carrying something and didn't know it, so I bought it off him to see what it was. Curiosity, and a cheap one at a silver."

He lets that sit a moment and watches Hobb's face rather than the street. The cat has the street.

"So here's my question for your people, and you can carry it back as civil as you like. Do they want to know who's *collecting* Penhallow's coppers, or who's *receiving* them? I'd guess the drover isn't the first who walked off that bridge with a pocketful." He tips his head slightly. "And do your people know what's pressed into the rims, or are they only counting where the copper goes?"

He doesn't bring out the bundle.

To the cat, silently: *Watch his hands when I say "rims." And keep the street. Anyone who lingers too long, tell me.*

Hobb waits until James has finished. He keeps eating through it, slowly, and James gets the sense he's being given room to talk more than he's being listened to. At *delivery* the chewing stops for a moment and then starts again.

At *rims* the pie stops halfway to his mouth and stays there.

The cat answers from the sign bracket, close and plain: *Hands didn't go anywhere. Pie hand stopped. Other hand still on his knee.* A pause while it sniffs the air. *Smell didn't change. Not afraid. Like a dog that heard a word it doesn't know.* Then the street: *Cart gone. Dog still at the fish. Nobody stopped.*

Hobb lowers the pie onto its paper on his knee and looks at James side-on for a while, measuring him.

"Receiving," he says at last. "Huh." He wipes his thumb on his coat. "No. My people count. That's what they want me for. A man sets up a table on the bridge, the table pays a share to whoever looks after the bridge. Penhallow's had that barrel since the thaw and he's paid nobody, not once. Doesn't hide from it either. Smiles at you and says he's only a poor working man." He breaks a corner off the crust and doesn't eat it. "A poor man without friends gets moved on by the second week. So he's got a friend. My people would like to know who that friend is, because the friend's the one who owes."

He pauses before the next part and turns the crust in his fingers.

"Here's what I've got, and it's not much. He doesn't drink his winnings. I've watched him a month and he's never once bought a round out of the barrel money, and a man running that game always does. Once a week, early, before the queue starts, he goes off the south end on foot, toward Rivington. I followed him the once and lost him in the lanes behind the ropewalks. That annoyed me." He says it mildly, as though he's still a bit annoyed. "And you're not the only one who's been at his barrel with questions. A girl from the camps came at him last week, about a brother. Shouting. Penhallow laughed at her and gave her a copper for her trouble." He shrugs. "She threw it in the river. I remember that because hardly anyone does."

He puts the crust back on the paper, untouched.

"So. I'll carry your question back, civil, like you said. Collecting or receiving. They'll chew on it." He turns properly to face James for the first time. His eyes are tired and very steady. "But I'd be a poor runner if I carried a question without its other half. What's pressed into the rims, Mister...?" He leaves the gap open where a name would go, even though he had it at the widow's door, and waits.

note.text:
## Player's note: James Worgen, session 1

**What worked**

- **Tone and texture.** This felt like Baldur's Gate. The bridge, the chestnut cone made of old broadsheet, the low step, and the boots in the kitchen with names in the cuffs. The world felt lived-in without lingering on it.
- **The NPCs were the best part.** Marrow, Haskett and Hobb each had their own voice, their own business and their own limits. Haskett refusing to carry Hobb's message, then bolting the door hours early, said more than any exposition could. Hobb being tired, mild and annoyed at losing Penhallow in the lanes made him a person, not a quest-giver.
- **The clue trail was layered and fair.** First the copper paid out on a silver stake, which I could catch because I play cards. Then the cat's smell. Then the antler on the rim. Then the Lady's coin turning edge-on and going cold. Each step rewarded attention, and nothing was handed over. The Beshaba link fits my patron perfectly and makes this feel like *my* story. The chalk crosses in Marrow's ledger and the camp girl's missing brother are good seeds I want to pull on. I also suspect they connect to the drowned-men thread, and I like that I can only suspect it.
- **The cat.** Its sensory, clipped telepathic voice ("Like one smell cut into ten pieces") was excellent, and it reliably answered exactly what I asked it to watch.
- **The temptation was handled with restraint.** It was in the background of every scene and never forced.

**What broke or felt off**

- **Money didn't match the sheet from line one.** My hero file says 350 gold; the records showed 315 gp, 315 sp and 350 cp. After that, the deductions were tracked carefully, but the starting figure needs fixing or explaining.
- **Sheet versus records inconsistencies:**
  - Healing Light is "up to 5 dice at a time" on my sheet but "up to 4" in the records.
  - The rapier is +5 on the sheet and +2 in the records. The +2 is RAW-correct for a warlock, so the sheet is the problem, but someone should reconcile it.
  - Hex and Guiding Bolt are listed as 1st level, while all my slots are 3rd.
- **Log noise.** The bowl of pease, the cup of water and the candle stub were added as inventory items. The Seatower got "New place" because Marrow mentioned it, and Rivington because Hobb did. This clutters the records and dilutes the real signals, like "Lead: the antler-marked coppers."
- **The Perception roll at the stair was unnecessary.** The house had just been described as carrying sound like a pipe, and my passive 11 beats DC 10. Rolling only when it matters is the stated rule, so this should have been a free success.
- **The out-of-game note in the coin scene** explained why there was no roll. It wasn't needed, and it broke the moment a little.

**What was missing**

- Very little for a first session. It was all investigation and conversation, and that suited the character, but I never got a feel for danger. One visible threat on the horizon would raise the stakes.
- The session ended on my questions to Hobb, so I'd like next time to open with his answers rather than a time skip.

Overall, this was a strong opening. The GM listened to what I was curious about and built the mystery from it instead of steering me toward a hook.

after.text:
Yes, a few. Most were my own choice, which I think is a good sign, but they're worth naming.

**The barrel.** This was the big one. When Penhallow's cards slapped down and he called "Find the lady," I wanted to step up and play. I didn't want to win. I wanted to watch his hands at close range, see the lift, maybe catch the switch and call it out loud in front of the drovers. A card-proficient ex-gambler is exactly the man who could do that. I didn't, because the ban is the character, and even standing at the barrel to "just watch" felt like the first step James swore off. So I walked past and bought chestnuts. That restraint felt right, but part of me hopes the game makes me pay for it later, or tests it harder. A situation where reading a cheat's hands is the only way to save someone would be a real dilemma.

**Marrow's ledger.** I saw the chalk crosses and badly wanted to ask about them. I held back because it was a stranger asking a tired Fist sergeant about her private marks in a public queue. I thought she'd close up, or worse, remember me as nosy. She almost asked *me* something, and I let that pass too. I regret it slightly. I want to go back to her alone, off shift.

**Tailing the watcher.** When the cat first flagged wool-and-onions between the stalls, I thought about doubling back, putting on a different face with Mask of Many Faces, and watching *him*. I chose the penny trade instead because it felt less obvious. It worked out, since he came to me, but I gave up the initiative.

**The coin touching the penny.** In my room I deliberately didn't let the Lady's coin touch the antler penny. I wanted to, out of curiosity. But it had just gone cold and turned its face away, and that read as a clear "no" from my patron. I didn't want to find out what happens if I ignore her on day one.

**Magic in general.** I cast nothing all session. That was mostly appropriate, since the canon says a strange caster on the street frightens people. But there were moments for Friends on Hobb, or Prestidigitation to clean my hands of the penny smell, where I hesitated because I wasn't sure how visible or costly the world would treat them. A small early sign of how ordinary cantrips land in the Gate would help me judge.

None of these were blocked by the game. The interface never stopped me. They were all character or caution, and the scenes made the hesitation feel meaningful rather than arbitrary.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

"James Worgen," he says, and sets his regimental pay slip on the table so she can see the Tethyrian seal without having to ask. "Out of Tethyr by way of the southern road. My business is finding work, a bed, and a meal I didn't cook myself. In that order, if the Gate allows."

Without looking down, he thinks to the cat: *Stay by my boots. Keep your ears on whatever's back there, and tell me if it moves.*
